text: On the half decayed veranda of a small wooden house near the edge of a ravine, outside Winesburg, Ohio, a fat little old man walked nervously up and down. <break time="0.8s" /> Beyond a long field, where clover had been planted but only yellow mustard weeds had grown, he could see the highway and a wagon full of berry pickers coming home. <break time="0.8s" /> The young men and women in the wagon laughed and shouted noisily, and a girls voice called to him, Oh, you Wing Biddlebaum, comb your hair. <break time="0.8s" /> The man was bald, yet his nervous little hands fluttered about his bare white forehead as though he were arranging a mass of tangled hair. <break time="0.8s" /> Wing Biddlebaum had lived in Winesburg for twenty years, but he did not think of himself as a part of the life of the town. <break time="0.8s" /> He was always frightened and troubled by a ghostly crowd of doubts, and among all the people of Winesburg, only one had ever come close to him. <break time="0.8s" /> That one was George Willard, a young reporter on the town newspaper, the Winesburg Eagle, with whom Wing had formed something like a friendship. <break time="0.8s" /> Now, as the sun went down, the old man walked up and down the veranda, hoping that George would come and spend the evening with him.
